issues.legal_issue: A police seizure of property without authority of law infringes constitutional rights and may be remedied by a writ directing restoration.
material_facts: Police seized medicinal herbs from the actual possession of the petitioner or his employees, without obtaining an order from a magistrate or another competent authority.
The seizure was made by local police at the request of police investigating an alleged offence in another territory, and no law authorizing the seizure was identified.
The provisions governing search and seizure by police did not apply to the circumstances of the seizure.
issues.conclusion: The seizure infringed the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 31 of the Constitution, and a writ directing restoration of the seized goods was warranted.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 19 and 31 of the Constitution, police may not seize a citizen’s property without authority of law; an unauthorized seizure infringes the citizen’s fundamental rights and may be remedied under Article 226. Sections 51, 96, 98 and 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 did not authorize these seizures. The Court also observed that, in view of Article 370, it was doubtful whether an offence committed in Jammu and Kashmir could be investigated by police in Himachal Pradesh. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenges_police_se: A person challenges a police seizure through a constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.police_took_goods_from_current_possessio: Police took goods from the actual possession of a person or that person’s agents.
predicates.no_law_authorized_seizure: No applicable law or lawful order authorized the police to take the goods.
predicates.unauthorized_seizure_infringes_fundament: The unauthorized seizure infringes fundamental rights and the goods must be restored.

issues.definition: When a person challenges a police seizure by constitutional writ, police took goods from that person’s actual possession, and no law authorized the seizure, the seizure infringes fundamental rights and the goods must be restored.

issues.legal_issue: A dispute over ownership or the lawfulness of possession does not permit police to seize property without authority of law or prevent relief for an unauthorized seizure.
material_facts: The goods were in the petitioner’s or his employees’ actual possession when police seized them.

Another person alleged that the goods belonged to a business connected with a partnership and that the petitioner’s brother had no right to transfer them; the petitioner and his brother denied those allegations.
The police seized the goods without authority of law.
issues.conclusion: Even if the petitioner was not lawfully entitled to possess the goods, they could not be seized except under authority of law; the disputed title did not prevent restoration of goods seized without such authority.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that property in a person’s possession cannot be seized merely because that person may lack lawful title or possession; seizure still requires authority of law. It applied Articles 19 and 31 of the Constitution and found that the search-and-seizure provisions in sections 51, 96, 98 and 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 did not apply. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.ownership_or_lawfulness_of_possession_is: Another person disputes the claimant’s ownership or asserts that the claimant was not lawfully entitled to possess the goods.

predicates.disputed_title_does_not_bar_restoration_: A dispute over title or lawful possession does not prevent restoration of goods seized without authority of law.

issues.definition: When goods in a claimant’s possession are seized without legal authority, a dispute over the claimant’s title or lawful possession does not bar their restoration.

issues.legal_issue: An unsuccessful application to a magistrate for return of seized property under an inapplicable procedure does not bar constitutional writ relief when the magistrate lacked jurisdiction.
material_facts: The petitioner applied to a magistrate for return of the seized goods under a summary procedure.
That procedure did not apply to the circumstances, and the magistrate had no jurisdiction to order the goods returned under it.
A challenge to the refusal of that application was dismissed on the ground that there was no jurisdiction to grant relief through that procedure.
issues.conclusion: The prior application and its dismissal did not prevent the petitioner from seeking relief under Article 226 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the return-of-property procedure in section 523 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 did not apply and that the magistrate lacked jurisdiction to return the goods under that section. Its inapplicability and the dismissal of the related challenge for lack of jurisdiction meant that this remedy did not bar relief under Article 226. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.prior_return_application_was_under_inapp: The person had already sought return of the property through a procedure that did not apply to the circumstances.

predicates.dismissal_of_inapplicable_return_applica: The dismissal of the return application does not bar relief through a constitutional writ.

issues.definition: When a person seeks return of police-seized property by constitutional writ after a return application under an inapplicable procedure was dismissed, the dismissal does not bar writ relief if the magistrate lacked jurisdiction to order return.
